_comment: The Revise layer: one byte-size card per syllabus sub-topic, for the tab beside Learn.
What this is. The notes teach a sub-topic in 250 words of continuous prose and the
revise layer (data/dcc_revise.json) already answers each SECTION in <=90 words. This
layer is a third thing: one card per SYLLABUS SUB-TOPIC - 1.1, 1.2, 2.3 - the same
size as every other, written in plain words with an emoji on the headline and one per
bullet, so the reading job for a unit is a number the reader can see before starting.
The fixed size is a contract, not a style note: every card is one lead paragraph plus
exactly four bullets, in BAND words, and tools/rev_summaries.py refuses a card outside
it. Emoji do not count towards the band - they are decoration, and counting them would
charge the reader four words a card for pictures.
Nothing is derived from the notes by machine (that was measured and rejected for this
material - see tools/dcc_slide_notes.json): each card is written by hand from the
sections that teach the sub-topic, and the same guard that watches the revise layer
watches this one - every bolded term and every quoted number has to appear in those
sections, so a card may compress them and may not add to them.
Keys are the syllabus's own numbering (data/syllabus.json is the authority: 34
sub-topics over nine units). Two cards are marked "prereq": 2.0 and 3.0 carry content
the unit's first sub-topic builds on, and the syllabus numbers neither. They are
declared here rather than folded in silently, and the guard allows exactly those two.
A card is a pointer as much as a summary: 120 words cannot carry every detail of a
sub-topic that runs to six sections, so it carries the answer and the named terms, and
the notes behind it stay one click away on the Learn tab.
> 9 units · 36 cards · ~120 words each · ~4 400 words for the whole course.
This file is the source. tools/rev_summaries.py --apply writes dcc-site/data/rev.js
(window.REV), which is what the page loads; --check fails if the two disagree.

1.1.html:
A distributed system is many computers that look like one computer to the user. Each machine works on its own, and they talk only by passing messages.

  • 🔑 Autonomous means each node has its own clock, makes its own decisions, and can fail on its own - nothing controls the whole set.
  • 📌 Three characteristics follow: concurrency (many jobs at once), no global clock, and independent failures, so partial failure has to be tolerated.
  • 🧩 Other properties are expected: heterogeneity, openness through published interfaces such as REST APIs, security, scalability, transparency and fault tolerance.
  • ✅ Good: cheap to add machines, easy to share resources. ⚠️ Bad: security is harder, data can be lost in transit, and the software is complex.

1.2.html:
Four goals shape a distributed system: resource sharing, openness, transparency and scalability, and each one answers a problem of its own.

  • 🔑 A resource is the thing itself. A service is the interface that manages related resources and decides who may use them and how. A file service offers read, write and delete on files instead of exposing the files.
  • 📌 Openness means standard rules and an interface written in an IDL, neutral about language and platform, which gives interoperability and portability.
  • 🫥 Transparency is a family: access, location, migration, relocation, replication, concurrency, failure and persistence.
  • ⚠️ The problems behind the goals are heterogeneity, reliability, security and scalability; middleware hides the first, and redundancy raises availability.

1.3.t: Examples: Google File System, Hadoop, BitTorrent, etc
1.3.html:
Three examples show the idea working: GFS, HDFS and BitTorrent. Each one splits data over many machines, and each machine serves what it holds.

  • 📁 GFS: one master keeps the metadata, files are cut into large chunks, and each chunk is stored on several chunk servers, typically three.
  • 🗄️ HDFS: a NameNode keeps the metadata and many DataNodes hold copied blocks - GFS plus MapReduce.
  • 🔁 BitTorrent: a file is cut into pieces, and every peer that holds pieces also sends them out, so no node's failure ends the sharing.
  • 🌍 The Web and systems like web search, online shopping and multiplayer games show the same problems: dangling links, slow response, and no proper user interface.

1.4.html:
Three architecture models say where the parts sit and how they relate: client-server, peer-to-peer and multitier.

  • 📞 Client-server: the client asks, the server answers with a result or an error, over send/receive or through RPC or RMI; one process owns the service, which is also its bottleneck.
  • 🤝 Peer-to-peer: every process is equal, no single failure ends the service, and the hard parts are placing objects, finding them and keeping copies equal.
  • 🏗️ Multitier: a presentation, an application and a data tier, so each layer can grow or be swapped on its own.
  • 🧠 Fundamental models describe what all architectures share - interaction, failure and security - and the types are cluster, whose key feature is homogeneity, grid and cloud.

2.0.html:
Distributed objects live in different address spaces, share data, and call each other's methods. The objects talk, not raw bytes, and location transparency is what that buys.

  • 📌 A local object and a distributed object are not the same: reference, request latency, object activation, parallelism, failure and security differ.
  • 🔗 Reference: locally it is one machine word, remotely it must mean something in another address space, which is why references are translated.
  • ⏱️ Request latency varies because every call crosses a network, the object may not exist yet, and several clients may call at once.
  • ⚠️ Failure is partial failure, which is why call semantics exist, and security is enforced by middleware rather than by the operating system.

2.1.html:
RPC lets a client call a procedure that lives on another machine. The client waits, blocked, until the server runs it and sends the result back.

  • 🔢 Ten steps: 1–3 client, 4–7 server, 8–10 reply. The client stub marshals the parameters at step 2, and the server stub unpacks them at step 5.
  • ✅ Gains: the procedure runs elsewhere, code is reusable, and the stub layer hides the network. ⚠️ Costs: call-by-value only, plus marshalling and round-trip overhead.
  • 🧯 Five faults: the server cannot be located, a lost request, a lost reply, a server crash and a client crash - fixed by a naming service, retransmission and duplicate filtering.
  • 📌 Call semantics: exactly once, at most once, at least once, last once, last-of-many. Repeats are safe only with an idempotent operation.

2.2.html:
RMI calls methods on an object in another process. RPC drops the object and keeps only the procedure name; RMI keeps the object.

  • 🔑 A remote call needs a remote object reference, a remote interface whose methods alone are callable from outside, and a remote object that implements it.
  • 🧩 Five roles: the proxy marshals, the dispatcher picks the method, the skeleton invokes it, the remote reference module translates references, and the binder maps names to references.
  • ⚖️ CORBA is neutral through an IDL; Java RMI extends Remote but both ends must be Java; both are at-most-once, and CORBA also maybe.
  • ⚠️ Full location transparency causes failure and latency, because a remote call is not a local call; the fixes are exceptions in the language or a weaker invocation semantics.

2.3.html:
Underneath RPC and RMI sit two mechanisms: the message-passing model, where the programmer writes the sends and receives, and serialization, which turns a value into bytes.

  • 🧠 Two memory models: shared memory is one data area that every element sees, while distributed memory gives each element its own, so data moves only in a message.
  • 📮 The work unit is the process, coordination is by send and recv with a tag and proc that may be wildcarded, and SPMD runs one program everywhere.
  • ⚙️ MPI wraps a program in MPI_Init and MPI_Finalize, gives each part a rank with MPI_Comm_rank, and moves data with MPI_Send and MPI_Recv.
  • ⚠️ Costs: copying into buffers at both ends, buffer space, packetization and tag matching. Short, eager and rendezvous protocols trade buffers against waiting.

2.4.html:
Sockets are the basic channel between programs on a network: the client's socket names a local I/O port, the destination machine and the server's port.

  • 📌 A read normally blocks; setSoTimeout sets a timeout, and after it the socket is still usable. Java offers Socket and ServerSocket.
  • 🔥 Web services exist because clients and servers sit behind firewalls. HTTP gets through, not because it is best, but because firewalls allow it.
  • 📦 Web Services 1.0 uses SOAP, with WSDL for the API and an XML envelope; Web Services 2.0 uses REST with GET, PUT, POST, DELETE and usually JSON.
  • ⚖️ SOAP needs WSDL and does more, but suits no browser client; REST is faster and simpler, and gives up the written contract.

3.0.html:
Every computer has its own clock, so there is no single clock to read. Clocks deviate, and that makes an execution hard to read as an order of events.

  • ⏱️ A timer is a counter register decremented by a quartz crystal oscillator; each interrupt is a clock tick, and the drift rate decides how often to synchronize.
  • 🐞 The classic failure is make: it uses its machine's clock, so with clocks out of step it may treat an output as newer than its source and skip a rebuild.
  • ➡️ The happened-before relation orders events by three rules - inside a process, send before receive, and transitivity - and unconnected events are concurrent.
  • 📬 Causal ordering holds a later message until the earlier one it waits for arrives; Lamport timestamps cannot decide this, vector clocks can.

3.1.html:
Clock synchronization has two families: physical clocks - Cristian's algorithm for a centralized system, NTP for a distributed one - and logical clocks, which count causality instead of seconds.

  • 🌐 Cristian's algorithm asks a time server whose clock comes from a radio clock or another accurate UTC source; the client sets its clock to T + RTT/2.
  • 🎯 Accuracy is ± RTT/2, improved by keeping the reply with the shortest round trip; the server changes time by slewing, not by setting it.
  • 📡 NTP servers listen on port 123 and reply with a UDP/IP packet carrying a 64-bit timestamp in UTC seconds since 1 Jan 1900; sources form a subnet of strata.
  • 🔀 Its modes are multicast, remote procedure call and symmetric at low, medium and high accuracy, and the offset comes from four timestamps.

3.2.t: Logical Clocks: Lamport's and Vector Clocks
3.2.html:
A logical clock is a counter that only goes up. Its value need not match any real clock; each process keeps its own and stamps events with it.

  • 📈 Lamport's algorithm has three rules: add one before each event, send the value with the message, and on receiving jump above the larger of the two.
  • 📌 It gives a total order over events, enough to order competing requests for one resource - but a smaller timestamp does not prove it happened first.
  • 🧮 A vector clock is an array of N counters, one per process: a send sends the whole array, and a receive takes the pairwise maximum.
  • ✅ Two events are causally related only when one vector dominates the other; BSS and SES use this to delay an out-of-order message.

3.3.html:
Two families decide who may enter a critical section: permission-based, where requests are arbitrated, and token-based, where one token goes round.

  • 🚦 A critical section is where a process competes destructively with another for a shared item; a race condition comes from two entering at once.
  • 📋 Four requirements: safety (one process inside), liveness, no starvation and fairness, with requests granted in order.
  • 💬 Ricart-Agrawala skips a reply when it holds a request with a lower timestamp, needs no FIFO channels, and costs 2(n − 1) messages per entry.
  • 🔑 In the Token Ring, n processes form a ring and the token takes 1 to n − 1 messages to arrive; if the holder dies, a process must be elected to remake it.

3.4.html:
Leader election picks one process to run a job spread over several nodes, and afterwards every node agrees on the same leader.

  • 🔢 Each active process has a unique priority number, and the coordinator is always the highest one, so a crashed node cannot win.
  • 👊 Bully elects the largest process ID where every process can reach every other, using an election message, an answer and a coordinator message.
  • 📨 A process that finds the coordinator down messages all higher IDs and elects itself if nobody answers in time; a recovered node then takes over.
  • 💍 Chang and Roberts works in a ring for any number of processes N without knowing the ring size, and the process whose UID returns is the leader.

4.1.t: DFS concepts: Transparency, Naming, Replication, Consistency
4.1.html:
A Distributed File System is a normal file system spread over many machines. Programs read and write files on other machines exactly as they do on their own.

  • 🧩 Eight concepts run through it: transparency, concurrency, replication, heterogeneity, fault tolerance, consistency, security and efficiency.
  • 🫥 The strongest form of transparency is access transparency: the same operations on a remote file as on a local one.
  • 🗺️ Naming maps names to files: host plus local name is neither location transparent nor location independent, a mounted remote directory is location independent, and one global name structure spans all files.
  • ⚙️ The service has a flat file service that acts by UFID and a directory service that maps names; consistency runs from strict to relaxed.

4.2.html:
SUN NFS (Sun Microsystems, 1985) was the first network file system to succeed commercially. HDFS is built for very large files on cheap hardware.

  • 🧊 NFS is stateless: each request carries everything the server needs, so nothing is lost when a server restarts.
  • 🧱 Its three parts are the protocol over Sun RPC and XDR, the server side with a file handle, and the client side.
  • 🐘 HDFS writes once and reads many times; files of hundreds of megabytes to terabytes are kept in blocks of 64 MB, copied three times.
  • 👑 A namenode holds the namespace and knows which datanodes hold each block, but data never flows through it; high availability pairs two namenodes with fencing.

4.3.t: Middleware: CORBA, Java RMI, Messaging MQTT, AMQP
4.3.html:
Middleware sits above the network and below the applications. It makes the network invisible and hides the hardware and operating system.

  • 🌍 It exists because distributed applications are heterogeneous: different parts, different vendors, and old systems that must keep working next to the new.
  • 🏛️ CORBA is a standard, not a product: an Object Request Broker defined by an IDL, with proxies, skeletons, GIOP messages and IIOP over TCP/IP.
  • ☕ Java RMI is middleware for one language only: the interface is the language itself, and a binder maps names to remote references.
  • 📮 MQTT is publish-subscribe messaging where a broker forwards data and a topic decouples sender from receiver; AMQP is binary, with queues and exchanges.

5.1.html:
Cloud computing has two definitions: the mechanism (shared pools of resources, ready in minutes) and the business model (computing sold over the Internet and billed by use).

  • ⚡ The utility idea is what separates cloud computing from ordinary hosting: pay for what is used, like electricity.
  • 🔬 Grid computing came from the National Labs in the early 1990s to pool resources for science; utility computing came from IT companies in 2005–2006 for business.
  • 🧱 Five technologies built it: distributed systems, virtualization, Web 2.0, service orientation and utility computing.
  • 🧭 Three axes keep the models apart: the service models SaaS, PaaS and IaaS, the deployment models public, private, community and hybrid, and the attribute elasticity.

5.2.html:
Cloud computing is on-demand, scalable and elastic: resources are shared, metered and charged by use, and elasticity is what makes it different from hosting.

  • 📊 Scalability is the ability to handle growth; cost-effectiveness comes from sharing one pool of resources among many users.
  • 💾 Two more characteristics are data storage and management: data sits closer to where it is used, and the provider runs maintenance and security, which is cheaper through specialisation and centralisation.
  • ✅ Benefits: shared CPU, storage and bandwidth, aggregation for data-intensive work, no capital investment for a private infrastructure, and peak demands that rarely coincide.
  • ⚠️ Challenges: availability of service, data confidentiality and auditability, vendor lock-in, a data transfer bottleneck and performance unpredictability.

5.3.t: Cloud service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
5.3.html:
The three service models form a stack. IaaS gives raw infrastructure - CPU, virtual machines and storage - and the customer may run anything on it, like Amazon EC2.

  • 🛠️ PaaS gives a platform to deploy applications with the provider's tools, and the customer controls only the application it deploys.
  • 📧 SaaS gives finished applications run by the provider, such as Gmail and Salesforce, with nothing installed locally.
  • 🧩 Four families of activity make up a cloud service: service management and provisioning, security management, customer services such as help and subscriptions, and integration services for data management and development.
  • 🔐 Provisioning covers virtualization, operations, QoS, billing and backups; security covers identity and authentication, cryptography, physical security, access control and firewalls.

5.4.t: Cloud deployment models: Public, Private, Hybrid, Community
5.4.html:
A deployment model is a choice about access and ownership: who may use the cloud, and who controls the machines it runs on.

  • 🌍 Public cloud: open to everyone or a large industry group, cheapest and easiest, and it suits demand that fluctuates, but it is weaker on security, control and reliability.
  • 🏠 Private cloud: used by one organisation only, also called internal or corporate, with little technical difference from a public cloud, and the most expensive to run.
  • 🤝 Community cloud: shared by organisations with shared concerns, so the cost is shared but capacity is fixed.
  • 🌤️ Hybrid cloud: two or more clouds joined by standard technology; de-perimeterisation removes the boundary, leaving identity and data-level security as the controls.

6.1.t: Basics of virtualization: Hypervisors (Type I & II)
6.1.html:
Virtualization runs several operating systems on one machine. A virtual machine is one isolated system with its own guest operating system and applications.

  • 🧩 Six kinds exist: application, network, desktop, storage, server and data virtualization.
  • 🎛️ A hypervisor, or virtual machine manager, sits between the hardware and the operating systems, giving each guest what it needs so guests cannot disturb each other.
  • 🧱 Type I runs directly on the hardware and is used in data centres (Xen, KVM); Type II runs as an application on a host system, as on a desktop.
  • ✅ Benefits: sharing, isolation, encapsulation, hardware independence and portability. ⚠️ The hypervisor is a single point of attack, where VM escape is possible.

6.2.html:
Both virtualize, at different levels: a virtual machine copies a whole machine, and a container shares the machine's operating system.

  • 🖥️ A virtual machine is software that emulates hardware; it runs on a hypervisor, on a host machine, and the guest can be a different operating system.
  • 🐘 A whole operating system is carried inside a VM, which is why an image is measured in gigabytes; it brings storage, memory and networking.
  • 📦 A container packs the code, its dependencies and its configuration into one image, and the engine keeps each container separate inside the same kernel.
  • ⚖️ Containers are lighter and start faster but are less secure, because the operating system is shared; VMs are heavier but isolated by the hypervisor.

6.3.html:
The reference architecture is the NIST model. Think of four layers, three management groups that cut across them, and six actors.

  • 🏛️ The layers are the service layer (SaaS, PaaS and IaaS), the resource abstraction and control layer (hypervisors and control software) and the physical resource layer of hardware and facility.
  • 📋 Cloud service management is business support, provisioning and configuration, and portability and interoperability; security, privacy and performance run vertically through all three layers.
  • 👥 The six actors are the consumer, who holds the business relationship with the provider, the provider, the auditor, the broker, the developer and the carrier.
  • 🤝 The broker negotiates between providers and consumers through intermediation, aggregation and arbitrage; the auditor verifies conformance to standards.

6.4.html:
Providers promise cloud services in SLAs, reserving enough CPU, memory and bandwidth for an agreed period. Getting that amount right is a business decision, not a technical one.

  • 📉 Underprovisioning breaks the SLA and costs penalties; overprovisioning wastes resources and loses money, so the amount reserved is always a compromise.
  • ❓ Five difficulties: unpredictable demand, hardware and software failures, heterogeneous services, power management and conflicting SLAs.
  • 🚚 In a cluster, provisioning needs fast installation of VMs, live VM migration and quick recovery; EC2 uses Xen and offers templates.
  • 🧠 Three methods: demand-driven by utilisation, event-driven for a known date, and popularity-driven for popular applications; cluster monitoring collects the cluster's status and a scheduler assigns tasks to nodes.

7.1.t: Overview of AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
7.1.html:
A cloud provider sells computing over the Internet by usage, and its platform is the whole catalogue of what it rents out.

  • 🏢 Three platforms matter: AWS (first, with EC2 using Xen and S3 for object storage), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.
  • 📚 All three now offer virtual machines, containers, functions and object storage, so the choice comes down to geography, price and ecosystem.
  • ✅ IaaS gives virtual CPUs and memory, storage, networking and load balancers; its gains are shared infrastructure, pay-as-you-use, on-demand growth and a focus on the core business.
  • ⚠️ Its costs: security is never total, upgrades are not made for every customer, and moving a virtual machine between providers is hard.

7.2.html:
S3 and Blob are object storage, and cloud storage comes in three shapes: object, block and file.

  • 📦 Object storage keeps objects in a flat space, each found by a key through an HTTP API; block storage is raw blocks attached to a VM; file storage is files in directories, shared by many instances.
  • 🪣 A bucket is the top-level namespace and the unit of policy and region, and the interface is REST: PUT, GET and DELETE on a URL.
  • 🛡️ Durability comes from replication and is separate from availability - S3 is designed for 99.999999999% - and access tiers trade retrieval cost against storage cost.
  • 🗃️ Database as a Service removes the administration - provisioning, maintenance, replication and tuning; relational and non-relational are the two families, with SimpleDB and Bigtable as the examples.

7.3.html:
Compute comes in three shapes, and each one leaves less work to the customer: virtual machines, containers and serverless functions.

  • 🖥️ Virtual machines (EC2, Azure VMs, Compute Engine) leave the operating system and patches to the customer; containers (ECS, AKS, GKE) leave the image; functions leave only the code.
  • 🔧 An instance is one running VM, an instance type its CPU and memory profile, an AMI the template it starts from, and a security group its firewall.
  • ⚡ Serverless means the provider runs the code: an event starts it, billing is per invocation, scaling is automatic, functions hold no state, and execution time is capped.
  • 🌐 All three providers converge because their services are APIs, and a platform is organised by region and availability zone, so copies survive one zone failing.

8.1.html:
Cloud security covers four things - data-in-transit, data-at-rest, multitenancy and data lineage - and three of them are states data can be in.

  • 🚚 Data-in-transit gets confidentiality and integrity from TLS or from encrypting the payload; multitenancy means the data must stay readable while it is processed.
  • 🛏️ Data-at-rest is usually not encrypted, because it is mixed with other users' data, so data remanence - data left where it was not meant to stay - is the risk.
  • 🔍 Data provenance goes further than lineage: integrity of data is not integrity of computation, because the bytes can be untouched while the result is wrong.
  • 🪪 Privacy covers collection, use, disclosure, storage and destruction of personal data (PII), and compliance follows the seven phases of the data life cycle, from generation to destruction.

8.2.html:
IAM is the set of policies and technologies that make sure the right people get the right access to the right resources.

  • 🔑 Authentication proves who someone is, from a password to multi-factor authentication; authorization decides what they may do.
  • 👥 User management handles accounts, groups and roles, with permissions attached to roles at cloud scale, and one identity across services is federated identity and single sign-on.
  • 🌍 In the cloud the organisation's trust boundary moves into the provider's domain, so it becomes dynamic and lies outside the organisation's control.
  • ⚠️ Access must serve employees, contractors and partners, often from mobile devices over networks nobody controls, so the control becomes identity rather than network location.

8.3.html:
An SLA is the contract with the provider: a minimum level and a target level, with metrics and objectives, and the usual remedy is a service credit.

  • 📝 A complete SLA names the service, the metric, the minimum, the target and the remedy when the minimum is missed; it is per service, not one document for everything.
  • 📊 The five criteria are availability as a percentage of time, performance as response time and throughput, disaster recovery as mean time to recover, problem resolution and data security.
  • ⏳ Availability is a percentage of a period: 99.9% of a thirty-day month is about 43 minutes of downtime, and 99.99% is about 4.3 minutes.
  • 🔄 The contract goes through definition, publishing, negotiation, operationalization and de-commissioning; a hosted application runs feasibility, on-boarding, pre-production, production and termination.

8.4.html:
The unit's reference is one table: eight common vulnerabilities, eight control areas, the shared responsibility model and one summary principle.

  • 🚪 The eight start with data breaches, insecure APIs where the API surface is the attack surface, misconfigurations such as open security groups, and account hijacking.
  • ⚡ Denial of service matters because elastic capacity can be billed to the victim; insider threats, shared technology risks and legal risks complete the eight.
  • 🔐 The controls are encryption in transit and at rest, identity and access management with least privilege and MFA, secure APIs, hardening configuration and monitoring.
  • 🤝 The shared responsibility model splits the duty: the provider secures the cloud, and the customer secures in the cloud - configuration, identities, data and code.

9.1.html:
Cloud computing gathered everything into data centres, and physics pushed some of it back out: sending every device's data to a distant centre costs latency, bandwidth and privacy.

  • 🪜 The move went from content at the edge, to edge servers helping, to fog computing, where end devices are part of the system.
  • 📶 The tiers differ by where the work sits: edge devices answer in milliseconds, fog nodes such as gateways and cell towers are one hop away, and the cloud is the elastic pool for heavy analysis.
  • ✅ What it buys: low latency for control loops, less bandwidth by filtering early, privacy by jurisdiction, and working while offline.
  • ⚠️ What it costs: many more nodes to manage, weaker physical security, updates across the whole fleet, and clock synchronisation between thousands of devices.

9.2.html:
Serverless computing means the provider runs the code and the customer runs no servers: execution is event-driven, scaling is automatic and billing is per use.

  • ⚡ FaaS is event-driven execution billed per invocation, with Lambda, Azure Functions and Cloud Functions as the platforms, and no server to patch.
  • 🧰 BaaS is the managed parts a function calls instead of running itself: databases, queues, authentication and storage.
  • ✅ It fits glue between services, scheduled jobs such as nightly reports, sporadic traffic such as a webhook, and event-driven workflows.
  • ⚠️ It is wrong for long-running processes, stateful services, latency-critical work where a cold start hurts, and steady high load, which is cheaper on a reserved machine.

9.3.html:
A container packs the code, its dependencies and the configuration into one image, and shares the host system kernel, which makes it lighter than a VM.

  • 🧾 The image is the packaged unit, the Dockerfile the recipe that builds it, and a registry stores and fetches images.
  • ❓ Many containers on many machines raise four problems: placement, restarting and self-healing, scaling, and discovery, because callers need a stable name.
  • ☸️ Kubernetes declares the wanted state and keeps working to match it; a pod is the smallest deployable unit and a service is a stable name in front of changing pods.
  • ⚠️ Isolation is weaker than a VM's: a kernel flaw crosses between containers, and hardening means a non-root user, dropped capabilities and a patched host kernel.

9.4.html:
Cloud-native treats the cloud as the given: the platform is elastic, programmable, failure-prone and disposable, so the application is built from small services.

  • 🧩 Its characteristics are microservices, containers, orchestration, declarative configuration, immutable infrastructure, continuous delivery, observability and horizontal scaling.
  • 🔪 A microservice owns its data and is deployed on its own, so scaling happens per service rather than for the whole application, and one fault stays contained.
  • ⚠️ The cost is distributed systems: consistency across services replaces transactions, partial failure becomes normal, and local calls turn into remote calls with latency and marshalling.
  • 🔗 Microservices need packaging, packaging needs orchestration, and many moving services need delivery and observability; the four trends are one arc from the cloud out to the edge.
